analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rate to 15 percent and adjusts asset values for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have cut the top capital gains tax rate from 28 percent to 15 percent, never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the tax rate on long-term investment gains from 28 percent to 15 percent for individuals and from 34 percent to 15 percent for corporations. It would have let sellers of stocks and business property adjust the purchase price upward for inflation before calculating the gain, and it would have raised the small annual limit on deducting capital losses for inflation. A half rate of 7.5 percent would have applied to capital gains of low- and middle-income taxpayers. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell stocks and business property after holding them more than a year. Because capital gains flow overwhelmingly to higher-income households, the bulk of the tax cut would go to wealthy taxpayers. Corporations selling assets would pay 15 percent instead of 34 percent on gains. Mutual funds, brokerages, and real estate sellers would also gain from a lower rate and inflation-adjusted basis.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top tax rate on long-term capital gains for individuals from 28 percent to 15 percent, with a 7.5 percent rate for the capital gains of low- and middle-income taxpayers.
Cuts the corporate capital gains rate from 34 percent to 15 percent.

Allows sellers of corporate stock and tangible business property held more than one year to increase the asset's tax basis by the rise in the gross national product deflator, so gains caused by inflation are no longer taxed.
Indexes the $3,000 (and $1,500) annual limit on deducting capital losses for individuals to inflation.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally or the deficit, since cutting the rate on investment gains and taxing away inflation gains would reduce federal revenue. Non-investors who keep paying full ordinary tax rates on wages would bear a proportionally larger share of the remaining tax burden.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury and wage earners generally

drawbacks.text: The tax cut would flow mainly to higher-income households, since capital gains are concentrated at the top of the income scale; the 7.5 percent rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers affects a small share of total gains.
Cutting the rate from 28 or 34 percent to 15 percent would reduce federal revenue, shifting the tax burden toward wages, which are taxed at ordinary rates and cannot be indexed.
The bill applies only to a narrow set of assets and includes no offsetting revenue provisions, so its full cost would show up as higher deficits or other taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Indexing basis for inflation has a fair logic: it stops taxing gains that are just inflation, not real profit. But the bill goes far beyond that, cutting the rate itself by roughly half for individuals and corporations, and the largest gains are earned by the highest-income households. The bill contains no offset, so its cost would land on other taxpayers or the deficit. The modest 7.5 percent rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers does not change where most of the benefit sits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on October 8, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill had one cosponsor, a Republican.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the existing 28 and 34 percent capital gains rates, and taxpayers generally were spared the revenue loss; investors gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut capital gains rates to 15 percent and index asset basis for inflation.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill, letting it die in committee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Republicans, but no committee or floor vote was ever taken, so no partisan division on the merits is recorded.

industries.industry: Investors and shareholders in stocks and business property
industries.note: The bill would cut their tax rate on gains roughly in half and stop taxing inflation gains. Because capital gains are concentrated among high-income households, the benefit would go mainly to the wealthiest taxpayers while revenue for public services would fall.

industries.industry: Financial services industry (brokerages, mutual funds, investment managers)
industries.note: A lower capital gains rate and inflation-indexed basis would make holding and selling investment assets cheaper, likely encouraging more trading and fund sales. The benefit is indirect and depends on investor behavior.
Corporate capital gains would be taxed at 15 percent instead of 34 percent when corporations sell assets. This lowers business tax costs while the lost revenue would be made up elsewhere.
The bill includes no offsetting revenue, so the Treasury would collect less, meaning either higher deficits or higher taxes on other income such as wages.
